# Project Deep Dive

[← Microsoft](../README.md) · [Every Microsoft question](../../microsoft.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/project-deep-dive-2)

`deep-dive` `impact` `leadership`

---

## Requirements

Select one project from your resume and walk through it from start to finish. The interviewer will lead 30-60 minutes of follow-up questions that probe:

- **End-to-end ownership**: did you define scope, build, ship, and measure results — or did you only touch a narrow piece. Candidates who give high-level slide-deck summaries without owning granular decisions are eliminated quickly.
- **Decision rationale**: every architectural and product choice faces a "why this, not that" challenge. Be precise about the alternatives you considered.
- **Trade-offs in hindsight**: "what would you change". The interviewer is evaluating technical maturity, not looking for an apology.
- **Impact quantification**: numbers (latency, cost, conversion, accuracy lift) plus the method used to obtain them. Order-of-magnitude is acceptable; "improved performance" without a figure is not.
- **Team contribution clarity**: "what did *you* personally write / decide versus the team". Microsoft interviewers are remarkably blunt about this and will pose the question outright.

The MAI loop variant of this round is tougher — multiple interviewers each spend 30-45 minutes on this format, drilling into different facets. The Azure / Office HE version is briefer and focuses more on scoping.

## Notes

The interviewer will not permit you to remain at the architecture-overview altitude. After 5 minutes of high-level storytelling, the questions zero in on:

- "Walk me through the exact code path that performed X."
- "What sat on the other side of the trade-off you described in step 3."
- "Show me the back-of-envelope arithmetic that drove the decision."
- "What broke in production and how did you debug it."

Project selection carries more weight than storytelling polish. Choose a project where you owned at least one non-obvious decision (eviction policy, schema migration, model architecture, latency budget allocation) and can defend the alternatives.

For MAI specifically: AI-collaboration questions arise organically — "how do you use AI to debug" / "did you use AI when building this". Interviewers are gauging fluency, not whether you employed AI.

## Preparation

- Choose one primary project and one backup. The primary should be the one where you owned the most non-obvious decisions, not the one that looks best on paper.
- Pre-write a one-page outline: problem, constraints, pivotal design decisions (with alternatives), implementation highlights, results with numbers, what you would change.
- Rehearse the "what would you change in hindsight" answer; this is the question most candidates stumble on.
- Be ready to sketch the system on a whiteboard from memory in 2 minutes; do not lean on slides.
- Have direct links to 1-2 representative PRs ready to share — some MAI deep-dive interviewers request a PR link and walk through the live diff.
- Pre-rehearse the explicit "what did *I* personally do" separation — Microsoft loops ask this directly.
